title: Long-span context affinity and kernel-fit notes
content:
Goal:
Quick investigative notes about how session affinity (token overlap across requests) interacts with kernel selection heuristics and MoE routing behavior for long-context workloads on Llama/Mistral/Qwen families. Trying to capture heuristics that could reduce tail latency regressions at ~4k-16k token regimes without sacrificing throughput.

Background/context:
- We've observed p95 spikes when many long sessions with overlapping prefixes hit the same expert sets (MoE) while the runtime switches kernels for different sequence lengths.
- Qwen and Mistral show different attention memory patterns vs Llama (chunking vs fused-attn kernels). Kernel-fit currently picks by sequence length + model shape; doesn't consider session affinity or recent KV cache locality.

Experiment setup (sanity):
- Cluster: 8x A100-40GB (numa aware), gds disabled, UVM toggled for subset.
- Models: llama-70b-v1, mistral-2-xl, qwen-14b. MoE variant synthetic with 32 experts emulated for routing stress.
- Workload: 60k requests over 1 hour, 35% long (8k-12k tokens), 45% medium (1k-4k), 20% short. Affinity sweep: 3 modes: high-prefix-overlap (80% share first 2k tokens), random, shifting (prefix rotates every 30s).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (generation end), per-token throughput, GPU mem utilization, kernel-switch counts, KV cache hit rate, expert fanout distribution. Traces collected with our per-request trace-id.

Observations:
1) Affinity -> Expert Hotspots: High-prefix-overlap causes ~2.3x concentration on a subset of experts. Hotspot experts show higher stall times due to FFN IO contention. When affinity is high, tail latency increases even though average throughput remains similar.
2) Kernel-switch churn: For long sessions where sequence length grows over time, we see frequent kernel-switch events as requests cross the kernel threshold (e.g., 1024/2048/4096). Each switch adds ~1.8-3.5ms overhead per request on average (depending on model family).
3) KV cache thermalization: With high-overlap workloads, KV cache warms quickly but suffers eviction churn when multiple concurrent sessions map to same KV shard. Qwen's attention layout makes KV lookups ~8% cheaper but more susceptible to eviction thrash under MoE fanout.
4) UVM impact: Enabling UVM for llama-70b reduced OOMs but increased p95 by ~12% under peak. Mistral benefited less from UVM due to its smaller per-token activation sizes.

Hypotheses and quick wins:
- Kernel selection should consider "session affinity banding": if many concurrent requests share large prefix overlap and likely to reuse same KV rows/experts, prefer a kernel that minimizes stall variance even if it sacrifices a small throughput percent. Essentially bias towards lower-switch, more stable kernel for high-affinity cohorts.
- Introduce a lightweight affinity score computed at enqueue time: overlap_ratio = (shared_prefix_tokens / avg_prefix_len) across N recent sessions. If overlap_ratio > 0.6 and estimated seq_len > 2k, pin that request to the current kernel variant for that session for X minutes or until prefix diverges.
- Expert-aware batching: When forming batches, prefer grouping by estimated expert set (cheap gating estimator) to reduce FFN IO spike variance. Even imperfect gating predictions reduce hotspoting by ~18% in sims.

Diagnostics (traces/examples):
- Example trace id T-20241118-439: 94% overlap across first 3.1k tokens, expert set concentrated on experts {3,7,21}. p95=410ms vs baseline 280ms. Kernel-switch occurred at token 1025 and 2049 adding ~4.1ms overhead overall.
- Heatmap: expert fanout vs latency shows a short tail where fanout>12 correlates with extra 20-40ms jitter depending on FFN kernel alignment.

Microbench results (summary numbers):
- High affinity mode, llama-70b: throughput -8% (tokens/s), p95 +27%, kernel-switch events +62%
- Shifting mode, mistral-2-xl: throughput stable, p95 +6%, KV hit rate lower by 12%
- Random mode, qwen-14b: minimal tail effects, but UVM increased p99 when memory pressure >85%

Tradeoffs and risks:
- Pinning kernels reduces dynamic adaptation benefits; could harm short-lived bursty sessions. Need TTL heuristics and fallback on capacity pressure.
- Expert grouping increases scheduling complexity and could increase batch latency for very low-concurrency customers. Use soft grouping and degrade gracefully.

Next steps / action items:
- (Ethan) Prototype affinity-score function in proxy enqueue path and add metric (affinity_ratio per queue). Target RFC in 2 weeks. Linked ticket RI-2145.
- (Priya) Run controlled microbench with affinity-based kernel pinning toggled, measure p95/p99 and throughput delta across model families. Aim for a/b test by 2024-12-09.
- (Jordan) Add gating-prediction shim to batcher that estimates top-3 expert candidates using a light-weight sketch of token histograms. Simulate on recorded traces to get expected reduction.

Open questions / things to watch:
- How does quantized kernel selection interact with affinity? We saw small regressions when switching from 4-bit to 8-bit kernels mid-session due to different FFN memory layouts.
- What is the right TTL for pinning? 30s vs 5 minutes had materially different effects on hit rate in our sim.
- Are there regulatory or safety impacts if affinity causes repeated exposure of similar outputs? (Raise with product).

Quick checklist for a follow-up run:
- [ ] Turn off UVM for baseline run, record MMR counters
- [ ] Run affinity sweep with 3 scales: 50k, 150k, 300k requests
- [ ] Collect per-kernel duration histograms and kernel-switch counts
- [ ] Attach gating distribution and expert fanout map

Notes-to-self: keep this doc informal. If follow-ups stabilize hypothesis, migrate to a design doc under product-hosted-api with experiments and rollout plan.

-- Jordan
